01

Who this trip suits

A Charleston marsh trip suits a visitor who wants an inshore redfish day shaped by tide and access. Tell the guide whether you want to cast lures, use bait or try fly fishing. Ask how much time each person can actively fish.

A beginner can request instruction and a seated option. A dedicated sight-casting trip may require a different tide, water level and skill than a general redfish outing. Ask the captain to describe that difference before you choose.

03

When to go

SCDNR describes red drum in South Carolina throughout the year. Juveniles use shallow estuary habitats and move into deeper inshore water in winter. Adult movements differ. Use that distinction when you discuss the target.

Ask the guide to choose a departure time around the actual tide and route. “Fall redfish” is not enough detail to justify a flood-tide marsh booking. The source does not establish a dependable Charleston monthly catch score.[1]

04

Choose the departure and check landing changes

County Parks lists Shem Creek in Mount Pleasant, Wappoo Cut in West Ashley and Folly Beach among the area’s public landings. These names are access choices, not verified charter meeting places. Confirm the actual dock and parking instructions with the captain.

A County Parks notice dated 4 November 2026 plans to close Remley’s Point in mid-November, with reopening expected in early summer 2027. Check the project update before travel. The notice identifies Shem Creek as an alternative during the closure; confirm current use and capacity.

The county warns that tides and currents affect ramps, with drop-offs possible at low tide. A public launch does not establish that a location suits wading.[2] [3]

06

What the guide provides: confirm in writing

Ask about rods, reels, bait or lures, landing equipment and fish-handling help. Confirm life-jacket fit, seating, shade, toilet access and the plan for children. Do not infer these features from a boat photograph.

Ask whether the quote includes a valid licensed charter operation and the passenger fishing coverage that applies. Request weather and cancellation terms separately. A marsh trip and an exposed nearshore replacement may not meet the same customer needs.[4] [5]

07

Local mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming a redfish photograph proves the same target and access on every outing.
  • Booking a fixed sightseeing time and expecting it to fit a specific marsh tide.
  • Using Remley’s Point without a current project and access check.
  • Confusing a public boat ramp with a safe place to wade.
  • Applying a rule or license exception from a different state.
08

Regulations and licenses

Use SCDNR’s current regulations directory for saltwater rules and the current guide edition. Confirm license coverage for the actual charter, or arrange the required personal license.

Check the current red drum rules and natural-bait tackle requirements through the authority pages. Do not rely on a remembered rule, a past-year table or an old photograph of a retained fish.[6] [4] [1]

Questions and answers

Can I plan a Charleston redfish trip all year?

SCDNR documents red drum year-round in state waters. The habitat, target size, tide and access change; confirm a specific plan for your dates.

Where should I meet a Charleston fishing charter?

Use the captain’s exact dock and map pin. Shem Creek, Wappoo Cut and other area landings are separate departures. Check the Remley’s Point project notice.

Is a flood-tide trip the same as any inshore charter?

No. Ask what tide and water level the proposed shallow-marsh method needs, and what happens if conditions do not fit.

LICENCE & PERMITS

Fishing licence for South Carolina

Anglers aged 16 or older generally need freshwater or saltwater coverage. A licence is required from the beach unless an exemption applies.

  • 14 consecutive days$11 USD
  • 1 year$35 USD
  • 1 day$10 USD
  • 7 consecutive days$35 USD
